statements.text: Visible light is the small part of the spectrum our eyes can see, so visible images show Earth much as we would see it.
Weather satellites use visible channels to track clouds, fog, haze, dust, snow cover and volcanic ash.
Plants reflect near-infrared light very strongly, so images that use it make vegetated land stand out.
Newly burned land reflects strongly in shortwave infrared, which makes it valuable for mapping fire damage.
In a common shortwave infrared, near infrared and green combination, water looks black, plants bright green, newly burned land red, and snow and ice bright blue.
A shortwave infrared band at 3.9 µm is sensitive to the hottest part of a fire, so GOES often detects fires before they are spotted on the ground.
Warm surfaces give off infrared radiation: energy absorbed by the ocean, for example, is re-emitted as infrared.
NOAA likens its infrared channels to night-vision goggles, because they see by day and by night.
Forecasters use cloud-top temperatures as predictors of rainfall intensity and flash flooding.
Most passive sensors cannot see through dense cloud, which is why maps of land temperature have gaps.
GOES has three infrared bands, at 6.2, 6.9 and 7.3 µm, that track water vapour in the upper, middle and lower atmosphere.
The VIIRS Day/Night Band is a single wide band, sensitive to visible and near-infrared light, that records Earth's lights at night.
Its signal includes city lights, lightning, fishing fleet lights, gas flares, lava flows and even auroras.
Moonlight reflected off ice, snow and other bright surfaces shows up too.
Microwave energy can pass through clouds, which many weather instruments make use of.
SMAP measures the amount of water in the surface soil everywhere on Earth, every 2–3 days.
Radar is an active instrument: it sends out pulses of energy and measures what is reflected back.
Synthetic aperture radar makes high-resolution images night or day, regardless of the weather.
How far radar reaches into a forest depends on its wavelength: a C-band signal only gets into the top layers of the canopy.
Altimeters are active instruments: they send pulses down to the surface and use the reflections to measure its height.
Satellite altimeters measure sea surface height over the oceans and coasts.
Sentinel-5P measures the atmosphere for air quality, ozone and UV radiation, and climate monitoring and forecasting.
Laser altimeters are active instruments: they send out pulses of light and measure what is reflected back.
GEDI uses laser ranging to measure Earth's forests and topography in high resolution.
Spectral resolution is an instrument's ability to tell finer wavelengths apart, with more and narrower bands.
EMIT uses this to map the minerals on Earth's surface in the regions that produce dust.
ABI detects visible and infrared light in 16 spectral bands.
It can capture a full-disk image every 10 minutes, the US mainland every five minutes, and smaller areas every 30 to 60 seconds.
Band 2 sees red visible light at 0.64 µm, and band 13, the clean longwave window, sees infrared at 10.3 µm.
AHI has 16 bands and scans the full disk every 10 minutes.
VIIRS measures 22 spectral bands from 0.402 to 12.49 µm, with pixels of 375 m and 750 m.
Its false-colour view combines shortwave infrared (band M11, 2.23–2.28 µm), near infrared (I2, 0.85–0.88 µm) and red light (I1, 0.6–0.68 µm).
It flies on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.
MODIS sees every point on Earth every 1 to 2 days, in 36 spectral bands from 0.4 to 14.4 µm.
Its daily land surface temperature product has pixels 1 km across.
MSI samples 13 spectral bands, from visible and near infrared to shortwave infrared: four at 10 m, six at 20 m and three at 60 m.
Its images serve land management, agriculture, forestry, disaster control and humanitarian relief.
OLI captures Earth's surface in visible, near infrared and shortwave infrared light.
TIRS measures two thermal infrared bands, 10.6–11.19 µm and 11.50–12.51 µm, with 100 m pixels.
It works at 5.405 GHz, a wavelength of about 5.55 cm, and images Earth day and night, regardless of the weather.
Its images are used to identify sea ice, detect oil spills and measure ground movement from earthquakes, volcanoes and landslides.
TROPOMI looks across a swath about 2,600 km wide.
Its products include nitrogen dioxide and methane.
SMAP launched with a radar and a radiometer. The radar stopped in early 2015 when its power supply failed, and the radiometer carries on.
OLCI measures the colour of the ocean and land in 21 bands, with 300 m pixels.

instruments.name: Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR)

statements.text: SLSTR measures global sea surface temperature to better than 0.3 K.
Sentinel-3 also makes fire monitoring products, such as fire radiated power and burned area.
SRAL is a dual-frequency Ku- and C-band radar altimeter that measures sea surface height for oceans and coasts.
SWOT is making the first global survey of Earth's surface water and measuring how water bodies change over time.
Its 120 km wide swath gives overlapping measurements over most of the globe, revisiting on average every 11 days.
ECOSTRESS makes high-resolution images of the temperature of Earth's surface, to learn how much water plants use and when they become stressed.
GEDI measures Earth's forests and topography with high-resolution laser ranging from the ISS.

instruments.name: Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT)

statements.text: EMIT is an imaging spectrometer that maps the composition of minerals on Earth's surface where dust comes from.
The ISS is an orbiting laboratory. 2 November 2025 marked 25 years of continuous human presence aboard it.
Earth-observing instruments mounted on the station include ECOSTRESS, GEDI and EMIT.
The first MODIS was launched on Terra in December 1999.
Since 2020, Terra has been drifting to an earlier equator crossing time, with no manoeuvres planned to hold it.
The second MODIS was launched on Aqua in May 2002.
NOAA-20 is part of NOAA's Joint Polar Satellite System.
NOAA-21 is part of NOAA's Joint Polar Satellite System.
Suomi NPP is no longer delivering new data. Its VIIRS record runs from 28 October 2011 to 2 November 2026.
GOES-19 operates as NOAA's GOES East satellite.
GOES-18 is NOAA's operational GOES West satellite.
GOES-16 now serves as an on-orbit backup.
Himawari-9 took over the main operational role on 13 December 2022, about 35,800 km above the equator near 140.7°E.
Himawari-8 has been Himawari-9's backup since 13 December 2022.
Together, the Sentinel-2 satellites revisit the equator every 5 days.

lessons.title: Light or heat?
lessons.summary: Compare GOES East's visible and infrared views, and see why one keeps working at night.

text.text: GOES-19 is NOAA's GOES East satellite. Its imager, ABI, detects visible and infrared light in 16 spectral bands.
This is band 2: red visible light at 0.64 µm. Visible light is the part of the spectrum our eyes can see, so this is much how the Americas would look to us.

question.prompt: Find the night side of the disk, if there is one right now. What will an infrared band show there?
choices: Nothing, just like the visible band

explain.text: NOAA likens its infrared channels to night-vision goggles, because they see by day and by night.

text.text: This is band 13, the clean longwave window, at 10.3 µm. Warm surfaces give off infrared radiation, so this band senses heat rather than reflected light.

steps.hint: If the whole disk is in daylight right now, the two views look alike. Come back in a few hours to see the night side.

text.text: Forecasters use cloud-top temperatures from infrared as predictors of rainfall intensity and flash flooding.
ABI can capture this whole disk every 10 minutes, so the views you see are close to live.

steps.hint: Switch between the two views to compare them.

lessons.title: Colours you can't see
lessons.summary: Use NOAA-20's shortwave and near infrared to find plants, burn scars and ice.

text.text: NOAA-20 carries VIIRS, which measures 22 spectral bands from 0.402 to 12.49 µm. This is yesterday's true-colour view of the whole Earth from VIIRS.

question.prompt: In a view that uses near-infrared light, how will forests and grassland look next to bare desert?

explain.text: Plants reflect near-infrared light very strongly, so vegetated land stands out.

text.text: This view combines shortwave infrared (band M11, 2.23–2.28 µm), near infrared (I2, 0.85–0.88 µm) and red light (I1, 0.6–0.68 µm).
Plants reflect near infrared very strongly, so the Congo rainforest and the Sahel's grasslands show bright green against the Sahara.

question.prompt: Antarctica is covered in ice. Ice reflects visible light but absorbs infrared. Which colour will it be?

explain.text: In a shortwave infrared, near infrared and green combination, snow and ice look bright blue, water black, and newly burned land red.

text.text: Newly burned land reflects strongly in shortwave infrared, which makes this kind of view valuable for mapping fire damage.

steps.hint: Between April and September, Antarctica is in polar night and shows black. Turn the globe to Greenland instead.

lessons.title: The orbit decides the data
lessons.summary: Why GOES sees one side of Earth every 10 minutes, while Terra sees all of it every day or two.

text.text: A geostationary satellite circles once in the time Earth takes to turn, above the equator, so it watches the same side of Earth all the time.
That is why GOES-19 can capture this disk every 10 minutes. It never sees the far side of the planet.

question.prompt: Terra flies low over the poles instead. How often can its MODIS camera see any one place?

explain.text: MODIS sees every point on Earth every 1 to 2 days, in 36 spectral bands.

text.text: Satellites in a polar orbit pass roughly over Earth's poles at low altitude, while Earth turns beneath them, so they see a different strip on every orbit.
This daily land temperature map is built from those MODIS strips. Clouds leave gaps, because most passive sensors cannot see through dense cloud.
It is difficult to combine every desirable feature in one instrument: a sharper view needs a narrower swath, which means more time between observations.
